column1: # YAML blocks in the documentation that belong to another product's
# configuration file rather than to an Antifailure manifest.
# Three tab separated fields: the page, the top level key, and why. A reason is
# required, because an exemption with no argument behind it is
# indistinguishable from somebody silencing a finding they did not understand.
# An exemption that stops being needed is reported, so this list cannot rot.

a load scenario document, not a manifest. The manifest names it under load.scenarios[].path and the engine parses it with load.ParseScenario.
the same scenario document. The window sessions start inside, so fifty of them do not arrive on one millisecond.
the same scenario document. What has to hold when the journey is over, judged by the load engine rather than by the manifest.

a GitHub Actions workflow, not a manifest. The page documents the trigger list the caller needs for `workflow_dispatch` to reach `af ci`, and `on` is the workflow key GitHub reads it from. `examples/github-workflow.yml` carries the same file whole.

a GitHub Actions workflow, not a manifest. The page documents the two permissions a job needs before GitHub will mint a workflow identity to exchange for an engine token: `id-token: write`, which GitHub withholds from a fork, and `contents: read`. It sits beside the `on` block above for the same reason.
a Continue config.yaml entry, not an Antifailure manifest. Continue reads this list to start local MCP servers, and the page shows its native format instead of pretending every client uses JSON.

a GitHub Actions workflow, not a manifest. The page shows the customer's whole workflow file, which is `examples/github-workflow.yml` verbatim, because a reader has to see that the file is short before believing that nothing else is required. `on` is the trigger list GitHub reads.

the same workflow file. The three permissions the job needs: `contents: read` for the checkout, `pull-requests: write` for the comment, and `id-token: write` so the job can prove who it is to a control plane without a stored credential.
the same workflow file. The one job calls the reusable workflow with `secrets: inherit`, which is the line the page explains, so the block has to be shown whole.

a GitHub Actions workflow, not a manifest. The page documents the one job in a customer's file, which calls the reusable workflow `.github/workflows/check.yml` with `secrets: inherit` and passes `toJSON(inputs)` on, and `jobs` is the key GitHub reads it from.

a GitHub Actions workflow, not a manifest. The page documents calling the action directly from a job of your own, with a service container and the checkout and permissions the reusable workflow would otherwise carry, and `jobs` is the key GitHub reads it from.

a Kubernetes Job, not a manifest. On the Helm chart the re-sealing tool runs once as a Job, and the page gives the whole object because every field in it is one an operator has to get right: the image, the command, the Secret keys it reads and the read-only root filesystem it needs a /tmp volume for.
the same Kubernetes Job. It names the Job the runbook's kubectl wait and logs commands address.
the same Kubernetes Job. It carries the pod security settings the chart's own jobs use and the env entries that read the migration connection and the sealing keys from the chart's Secrets.

the custom roles policy file an organization applies with PUT /roles/policy, not a manifest. It is the enterprise edition's own format: fromYAML in ee/web/rbac/src/policyfile.ts parses it, and it is exported from and applied to the control plane rather than committed to the repository under test.
the same custom roles policy file. The named sets of repositories a grant can be scoped to.
the same custom roles policy file. Each grant gives one member one custom role at one scope.
the same custom roles policy file. The page shows the section empty, because a file carrying an approval policy is refused whole.
